raw_case_text:
A 55-year-old woman from Eastern Asia had been living in Europe for many years and underwent LC for cholecystitis. Her past medical history included asthma, no previous laparotomy, and abdominal pain for 5 months. Twenty days before LC she was admitted for jaundice to a medical unit, where abdominal percutaneous ultrasound examination showed a thick walled (9 mm) gallbladder with an obstructing gallstone impacted in the infundibulum, without dilation of intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts. The last time she had been to her native country was one year before; biochemical tests demonstrated that the alanine aminotransferase (AST) level was within the normal ranges of 3-45 U/L, the total bilirubin level was 4 mg/dL (nonconjugated bilirubin 3.3 mg/dL), coagulation tests and platelets were normal; the markers of hepatitis B and C were negative, the white blood cells count was normal (8.000/mmc), the eosinophils count was normal, and Entamoeba Histolytica was absent in stool: consequently, no infectious disease was found, and the cause of jaundice remained unexplained. Endoscopic retrograde cholangio pancreatography (ERCP) with endoscopic papillotomy had definitely ruled out obstruction of the biliary tree, while laboratory tests confirmed the persistence of nonconjugated bilirubin values comprised between 3 and 3.5 mg/dL; insofar her jaundice was attributed to Gilbert's disease. Besides, in a fortnight, she became asymptomatic and was discharged. Elective LC was scheduled, but another twenty days later, she complained again of abdominal pain in the upper right quadrant and was admitted to our surgical unit where we decided to perform LC in emergency. Because the walls of gallbladder were thick and cohesive, dissection by monopolar coagulation from liver bed was demanding and took longer time than usually. No intraoperative complication occurred, and after excision of the gallbladder, intraoperative cholangiography was carried out by laparoscopy, confirming the complete patency and normality of the biliary tree and the absence of stones in bile ducts. The early postoperative course of operation was uneventful, and the patient was discharged 5 days after surgery. The histologic examination was consistent with acute inflammation arisen in the context of lithiasic chronic cholecystitis. Oral feeding continued at home, the patient remained asymptomatic for 2 weeks, until she referred a mild epigastric pain irradiated to the right quadrant, but she did not see a doctor; one week later, she experienced sudden hypotension with melena and was admitted to our emergency service. Blood pressure was 100/60 mmHg, pulse rating was 86 beats/minute, haemoglobin level was 8 gr/dL, hematocrit level was 23%, white blood count was 9.700/mmc, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) level was increased to 838 U/L (normal values 3-45), aspartate aminotransferase (AST) level was elevated to 190 U/L (normal values 0-40), alkaline phosphatase level was within the normal and ranges of 35-129 U/L, coagulation tests and platelets were normal, total bilirubin level was 3.5 mg/dL. Digestive endoscopy showed the presence of blood in the upper gastrointestinal tract, without evidence of ulcers or other diseases causing bleedings from stomach or duodenum. Abdominal computed tomography (CT) showed a small haematoma of 3 cm in the gallbladder bed with no hemoperitoneum or any other peritoneal fluid collection and a iatrogenic pseudoaneurysm of RHA beside titanium clips sized 4 mm without arterial blushing. Resuscitation with transfusional support (3 units of packed red blood cells) allowed the patient to reach hemodynamic stability, then she was sent to our surgical ward.
Haemoglobin level increased to 12 gr/dL and hematocrit level to 36%. We excluded surgical primary repair because of the high risks related to possible misinterpretation of anatomy after 3 weeks of local inflammation. Further intermittent episodes of melena occurred in the following days anyway, with hemodynamic stability and minimal decrease of Hb and Ht levels; white blood cells count was 11.000/mmc, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) level lowered to 192 U/L and aspartate aminotransferase to 141 U/L, while the total bilirubin level raised to 12 mg/dL with 2.6 mg/dL of nonconjugated bilirubin. Since the patient persisted stable in hemodynamic parameters without fever or abdominal pain or tenderness, we planned to perform angiography only in case of rebleeding, so much more because CT had not shown any arterial blushing, which could make angiography inconclusive. The patient underwent ERCP that demonstrated a biliary leak in the gallbladder bed at the level of the biliary branch for the V segment; therefore, a nasobiliary drainage (NBD) was placed. Two days later, another episode of severe melena with hemodynamic instability occurred; hence, transfemoral angiography was performed, revealing the presence of a pseudoaneurysm sized 2 cm sited on a replaced RHA with extravasation between the V and VIII segmental branches (Figure 1); RHA was an arterial branch arising from the superior mesenteric artery: TAE was achieved by filling the entire artery and pseudoaneurysm with coils of 3 and 4 mm (Figure 2). The patient had an uneventful clinical course without rebleeding, and the NBD was removed and started oral intake. A CT scan proved revascularization of the right hepatic arterial branches with no ischaemia of the right liver lobe. The patient was discharged 2 weeks later with no impairment of liver function tests, and a magnetic resonance cholangiography showed a normal biliary tree.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 55-year-old East Asian woman presented with acute upper right quadrant abdominal pain requiring emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy, followed 3 weeks postoperatively by sudden hypotension and melena.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had a 5-month history of abdominal pain and was initially hospitalized 20 days before surgery for painless jaundice (attributed to Gilbert's syndrome after ERCP with papillotomy excluded biliary ductal stones and abdominal ultrasound showed a thick-walled 9-mm gallbladder with an impacted infundibular gallstone). Twenty days after discharge, recurrent right upper quadrant pain prompted emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy (complicated by difficult monopolar dissection of a thick, cohesive gallbladder wall; pathology showed acute-on-chronic calculous cholecystitis). Two weeks postoperatively she developed mild epigastric pain radiating to the right upper quadrant, followed 1 week later by sudden hypotension and melena requiring emergency readmission.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of asthma and Gilbert's disease; no prior laparotomies before laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Originally from Eastern Asia, living in Europe for many years, with last travel to her native country 1 year prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for right upper quadrant/epigastric abdominal pain, prior jaundice, and postoperative melena and dizziness/hypotension. Negative for fever on readmission.

objective.physical_examination: Readmission vital signs: blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, pulse 86 beats/min, afebrile, without abdominal pain or tenderness after initial stabilization.
objective.routine_investigations: Pre-cholecystectomy workup: AST normal (3-45 U/L), total bilirubin 4 mg/dL (unconjugated 3.3 mg/dL), normal coagulation and platelets, WBC 8,000/mmc, normal eosinophils, negative hepatitis B and C markers, and negative stool examination for Entamoeba histolytica; abdominal ultrasound showed a 9-mm thick-walled gallbladder with an impacted infundibular stone. Readmission labs (3 weeks post-LC): hemoglobin 8 g/dL, hematocrit 23% (improving to Hb 12 g/dL and Ht 36% after 3 units PRBC transfusion), WBC 9,700/mmc (later 11,000/mmc), ALT 838 U/L (normal 3-45 U/L; later 192 U/L), AST 190 U/L (normal 0-40 U/L; later 141 U/L), normal ALP (35-129 U/L), normal coagulation/platelets, and total bilirubin 3.5 mg/dL (rising to 12 mg/dL with 2.6 mg/dL unconjugated during intermittent melena).
objective.advanced_workup: Preoperative ERCP with endoscopic papillotomy and intraoperative laparoscopic cholangiography showed a patent, stone-free biliary tree. Readmission upper GI endoscopy showed blood in the upper GI tract without gastroduodenal ulcers. Abdominal CT revealed a 3-cm gallbladder bed hematoma without hemoperitoneum and a 4-mm iatrogenic right hepatic artery (RHA) pseudoaneurysm adjacent to titanium clips without active arterial blush. Repeat ERCP demonstrated a segment V biliary branch leak in the gallbladder bed, managed with nasobiliary drainage (NBD). Following recurrent severe melena and hemodynamic instability 2 days later, transfemoral angiography identified a 2-cm pseudoaneurysm on a replaced RHA (arising from the superior mesenteric artery) with active extravasation between segmental branches V and VIII.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Transfemoral angiography and ERCP confirmed hemobilia secondary to a ruptured 2-cm iatrogenic pseudoaneurysm of a replaced right hepatic artery (RHA) communicating with a segment V biliary leak following laparoscopic cholecystectomy (with infectious causes including Entamoeba histolytica and viral hepatitis ruled out during initial jaundice workup). Management included transfusion of 3 units of packed red blood cells, endoscopic nasobiliary drainage (NBD), and selective transcatheter arterial embolization (TAE) of the replaced RHA and pseudoaneurysm using 3-mm and 4-mm microcoils. Follow-up CT confirmed collateral revascularization of the right hepatic lobe without ischemia, NBD was removed, and she was discharged 2 weeks later with normal liver function tests and a normal biliary tree on MRCP.
